items.plain: When you work for others, don't chase fame; when you work for yourself, avoid shame. Keep to the middle way, and you will stay healthy in body and mind, do your duties, and live out your natural life.
items.core_idea: Keep to the middle way, avoiding fame and disgrace

items.plain: A good cook replaces his knife yearly because he slices; an ordinary cook monthly because he hacks. This cook has used one knife for nineteen years on thousands of oxen, and it is still as sharp as new.
items.core_idea: Skill that works with things wears nothing out

items.plain: Wild birds have to search hard for every bite and every drink, yet they don't want to be fed in a cage. In a cage they would have food on demand, but they would not be free.
items.core_idea: Freedom is worth more than easy comfort

items.plain: The Master was born when his time came and died when his time came. Accept birth and death like that, and grief has no place. The fuel burns out, but the fire may pass on endlessly.
items.core_idea: Accepting birth and death in their time ends grief

items.plain: The wise people of old first found the Tao for themselves and only then shared it with others. Until you have it yourself, you have no time to spare for dealing with what wicked people do.
items.core_idea: Find the Tao yourself before trying to fix others

items.plain: Listen not with your ears or mind but with your soul. Let hearing and thinking stop, so the soul is empty and simply responds. Only the Tao lives in that emptiness; this is fasting of the heart.
items.core_idea: An empty, receptive heart is where the Tao lives

items.plain: The highest virtue is to tend your own heart so that neither joy nor sorrow takes hold of it, and to learn to accept what cannot be avoided.
items.core_idea: Highest virtue is calm acceptance of the inevitable

items.plain: An official often faces situations he cannot control. But if he simply sticks to his work and forgets himself completely, he has no time left to cling to life or dread death.
items.core_idea: Absorption in your work frees you from fear of death

items.plain: Contests start friendly and end hostile; parties start orderly and end in drunken chaos, because things are pushed too far. Everything is like this: it begins in good faith and ends in contempt. Small beginnings lead to big endings.
items.core_idea: Things pushed too far turn from good faith to contempt

items.plain: Words stir people up as wind stirs waves, and actions easily drift from their aim. So anger flares for no clear reason, and dishonest arguments follow. When you push someone too far into a corner, they will always fight back.
items.core_idea: Push someone into a corner and they will resist

items.plain: The praying mantis raised its arms to stop a chariot, not knowing it was far too weak, so proud was it of its energy. Be careful: if you keep offending people by acting superior, you will probably come to harm.
items.core_idea: Showing off your superiority leads to harm

items.plain: People who love horses pamper them. But when a groom suddenly swats a fly off a horse, the startled animal breaks its bridle and hurts itself. The intention is good, but real care for the horse is missing.
items.core_idea: Good intentions are not the same as real care

items.plain: Trees of every size are cut down for useful things: monkey cages, house beams, rich men's coffins. So they never live out their years. Being valuable brings this misfortune.
items.core_idea: Being useful can cut your life short

items.plain: The honours of this world weigh as little as feathers, yet nobody sees how little they are worth. The troubles of life weigh as much as the earth, yet nobody can escape them.
items.core_idea: Honours are light; misfortunes are heavy and unavoidable

items.plain: Many people with toes laughed at me for having none, and it used to make me angry. Since studying with our Master I no longer care; I have been with him nineteen years without even noticing the missing toes.
items.core_idea: Inner growth makes others' mockery stop mattering

items.plain: Whoever knows what God is and what Man is has arrived: he knows he came from God, rests in what is known, and waits for the unknown. Living out your full span is the fullness of knowledge.
items.core_idea: Knowing God and Man, rest and live your span

items.plain: The pure people of old acted without scheming and didn't chase results. They made no plans, so when they failed they had nothing to regret, and when they succeeded nothing to boast about.
items.core_idea: Acting without scheming leaves no regret or pride

items.plain: The pure people of old slept without dreams and woke without worry. They ate whatever came and breathed deeply, for the pure breathe from their very depths, while common people breathe only from their throats.
items.core_idea: The pure live calmly and breathe from deep within

items.plain: The pure people of old neither loved life nor hated death; they came and went. Not forgetting their origin, nor rushing back to it, they cheerfully played their parts and waited patiently for the end.
items.core_idea: Live your part cheerfully, neither clinging nor rushing

items.plain: Wetting stranded fish with breath or spit is nothing compared with leaving them in their rivers to begin with. Likewise, better than praising good rulers and blaming bad ones is to leave both and develop the Tao.
items.core_idea: Better to live naturally in the Tao than be rescued
items.extended_text: When the pond dries up, and the fishes are left upon dry ground, to moisten them with the breath or to damp them with spittle is not to be compared with leaving them in the first instance in their native rivers and lakes. And better than praising Yao and blaming Chieh would be leaving them both and attending to the development of TAO.

items.plain: The Tao gives me my body, my work as an adult, my rest in old age, and my rest in death. Whatever arranges my life so kindly is also the best judge of my death.
items.core_idea: Trust the Tao that shapes your life with your death

items.plain: Being born human is always a reason for joy. And then to go through countless changes, with only the infinite ahead of you, is a happiness beyond compare.
items.core_idea: Being human, and endlessly changing, is great joy

items.plain: Metal demanding to be made a famous sword would be rejected by the smith; so would I by God if I demanded to be a man again. The universe is the furnace, God the smith; I'll go wherever I'm sent.
items.core_idea: Accept whatever form God makes of you

items.plain: A lament sung over a dead friend: will you come back to us, Sang Hu? You have already returned to your God, while we remain here as men, alas.
items.core_idea: The dead friend has returned to God; we remain

items.plain: My parents wouldn't want me poor, and Heaven and Earth treat everyone equally, so why single me out? I searched for the cause and found none. So it must be Destiny that brought me here.
items.core_idea: Hardship no one chose must be Destiny

items.plain: The perfect person uses the mind like a mirror: it grabs at nothing and refuses nothing; it reflects but does not hold on. So he can deal with the world without being harmed by it.
items.core_idea: Use the mind like a mirror: reflect, don't hold

items.plain: Two rulers, treated kindly by their host Hun Tun, wanted to repay him. Seeing he had none of the seven openings people have for senses, they bored one hole a day; on the seventh day Hun Tun died.
items.core_idea: Forcing others into your mould can destroy them

items.plain: The one seeking perfection keeps to his own nature. A duck's short legs can't be stretched, nor a crane's long legs cut, without pain; so what is long or short in our moral nature shouldn't be altered.
items.core_idea: Don't force your nature to be other than it is

items.plain: True hearing is hearing yourself, not others; true seeing is seeing yourself, not others. Someone who watches others instead of himself takes hold of their lives rather than his own, and ends up becoming someone else instead of himself.
items.core_idea: Watch yourself, not others, to stay yourself

items.plain: Everyone strains to grasp what they don't know, but no one works on what they already know; and everyone runs down what they aren't good at, but no one questions what they are good at.
items.core_idea: People chase the unknown and dismiss what they lack

items.plain: Great joy pulls a person to one extreme, deep sorrow to the other, and when that balance is upset, nature and the body suffer. Swung between joy and sorrow, people lose their steadiness and fail in thought and action.
items.core_idea: Extremes of joy and sorrow throw you off balance

items.plain: Gentleness can soften the hardest heart, but try to cut and shape it and it blazes or freezes. In an instant it reaches the ends of the earth; nothing can lock or bind it. Such is the human heart.
items.core_idea: The human heart yields to gentleness, never to force

items.plain: See nothing and hear nothing; let your soul rest in quiet, and your body will take its proper shape. Keep total stillness and purity, don't tire your body or disturb your energy, and you will live for ever.
items.core_idea: Deep stillness and purity preserve body and soul

items.plain: Treasure what is inside you and shut out what is outside, because too much knowledge is a curse.
items.core_idea: Guard your inner life; much knowledge is a curse

items.plain: Rest in not-doing, and the world will become good by itself. Shed your old skin, spit out cleverness, ignore differences, become one with the infinite. Let your mind go, free your soul, be empty, be Nothing.
items.core_idea: Let go of doing and cleverness; become one with all

items.plain: People like those who resemble them and dislike those who don't. Befriending only your own kind comes from a wish to stand out from others. But driven that way, how can anyone actually stand out?
items.core_idea: Sticking to your own kind won't make you distinct

items.plain: Moving and resting, living and dying, rising and falling are not under a person's control. But working on yourself is in your own hands.
items.core_idea: Life's events aren't yours to control; self-cultivation is

items.plain: Don't you study to look like a sage, talk big to rise above others, and seek fame? Instead, forget yourself and drop the body's chains. If you can't govern yourself, how can you govern an empire?
items.core_idea: Govern yourself before presuming to govern others

items.plain: Call a man a flatterer and he's angry, yet he always is one. The world loves such pretence. To pose and agree with everyone to win favour, yet deny being a flatterer, is the height of folly.
items.core_idea: Pleasing the world while denying it is folly

items.plain: A fool who knows he is a fool is not a great fool; someone who knows he is wrong is not badly wrong. Great error can never be shaken off, and a great fool never sees clearly.
items.core_idea: Knowing your folly means you're not a great fool

items.plain: If I know I can't succeed and still force it, that is just another mistake. So it is better to stop striving. But if I don't strive, who will?
items.core_idea: Forcing hopeless success is error, yet someone must try

items.plain: The sage's calm comes from his state of mind, which nothing can upset. Still water is a clear mirror; a still mind is clearer still. The sage's quiet mind becomes a mirror of the whole universe.
items.core_idea: A still mind mirrors the whole universe

items.plain: If people describe you truthfully and you reject it, you only double the blame. My humility is natural; it is not humility put on for its own sake.
items.core_idea: Accept true descriptions; real humility is natural

items.plain: You are too sure of yourself, too hasty, and you rate your own abilities too highly. People like that are not trusted.
items.core_idea: Overconfidence and haste make people distrust you

items.plain: Making a wheel, too slow and it's weak, too fast and the spokes won't fit; mind and hand must work as one. Words can't explain the knack, so I can't teach my son, and at seventy I'm still making wheels.
items.core_idea: Real skill cannot be put into words or taught

items.plain: A boat suits water and a cart suits land; push a boat on land and it won't move. Past and present are like water and land. Forcing old customs onto new times brings hard work, no result, and self-harm.
items.core_idea: Forcing old ways on new times only causes harm

items.plain: A great beauty frowned when she was upset. An ugly village woman, seeing how lovely she looked, copied the frown, and everyone fled from her. She saw that the frown was beautiful but not what made it beautiful.
items.core_idea: Copying the outward form misses its true source

items.plain: Those who live for wealth can't bear losing money; those who live for status can't bear losing fame; the power-hungry won't share authority. Anxious holding on, miserable losing, never learning from the past, such people are cursed by God.
items.core_idea: Living for wealth, fame or power brings endless anxiety

items.plain: The snow goose is white without washing, the raven black without dyeing; natural simplicity needs no argument, and fame isn't worth enlarging. Wetting stranded fish is nothing compared with leaving them in their rivers.
items.core_idea: Natural simplicity beats artificial effort and fame

items.plain: If the body works without rest, it dies. If the mind is used without a break, it gets tired, and once tired it loses its power.
items.core_idea: Body and mind both need rest to keep their power

items.plain: Getting what you want once meant complete happiness; now it means an office, which is outside you and comes and goes beyond your control. Don't treat office as fulfilment or fawn when poor; be equally happy always, and sorrow ends.
items.core_idea: Be equally content whatever position or poverty brings

items.plain: You can't talk about the ocean to a frog in a well, whose world is too small, or about ice to a summer insect, which lives one season. And you can't talk about the Tao to a narrow-minded schoolmaster.
items.core_idea: Narrow minds cannot grasp what lies beyond them

items.plain: Space and time are endless, and nothing is fixed. So the wise man is not elated by success or crushed by failure, does not grieve the far past, and neither celebrates life nor resents death.
items.core_idea: Seeing the endless whole frees you from elation and grief

items.plain: What a person knows is nothing compared with what he doesn't, and his lifetime is nothing compared with the time he doesn't exist. When the small tries to take in the great, it only ends in confusion and failure.
items.core_idea: The small mind cannot exhaust the infinite

items.plain: The Tao has no beginning or end. Everything else is born, dies, and keeps changing for better or worse. The past can't return and time can't stop; every end is followed by a new beginning.
items.core_idea: Everything changes; every end begins something new

items.plain: Fishermen brave sea monsters, hunters brave tigers, and heroes face death in battle as calmly as life. But the sage's courage is knowing that failure is fate and success is opportunity, and staying fearless in great danger.
items.core_idea: True courage accepts fate and stays fearless

items.plain: Offered high office, Chuang Tzu asked whether a sacred tortoise would rather be dead and honoured in a temple or alive, wagging its tail in the mud. Alive, they said. Go, then: I'll wag my tail in the mud.
items.core_idea: Better a free, humble life than an honoured cage

items.plain: I don't know whether what the world calls happiness is real. Ordinary people's happiness seems to be blindly following the crowd as if they had no choice. Yet they all say they are happy.
items.core_idea: Following the crowd may not be real happiness

items.plain: After his wife died, Chuang Tzu sang and drummed on a bowl. He grieved at first, then remembered she had passed from formlessness to life to death like the seasons; wailing would show ignorance of nature's laws.
items.core_idea: Death is a natural change, like the seasons

items.plain: Life is a loan that only adds more dust to the world. Life and death are like day and night. Seeing death all around us, if it comes for me too, why should I hate it?
items.core_idea: Life and death are like day and night

items.plain: Those who understand life don't bother with what life cannot achieve. Those who understand destiny don't bother with what knowledge cannot control.
items.core_idea: Don't spend yourself on what you can't control

items.plain: Someone taking revenge doesn't break the weapon that did the killing, and even the most spiteful person doesn't hold a grudge against a tile that fell on his head.
items.core_idea: No one resents a thing that harms without intent

items.plain: A man betting for tokens plays well; bet his belt and he gets nervous; bet gold and he loses his head. His skill hasn't changed, but the stakes distract him. Anyone who values outside things becomes empty inside.
items.core_idea: Caring about external stakes ruins inner skill

items.plain: I go down with the whirlpool and come up with the current. I adapt myself to the water, not the water to me. That is how I can handle it.
items.core_idea: Adapt to the current instead of fighting it

items.plain: First I make my mind completely still. After three days I forget reward, after five fame, after seven my own body. Then, with no thought of the court, my skill is focused and all distraction is gone.
items.core_idea: Stilling the mind removes distraction and focuses skill

items.plain: Forgetting your feet means the shoes fit; forgetting right and wrong means the heart is at ease. No inner change and no yielding to outside pulls is ease in every situation, and true ease forgets it is easy.
items.core_idea: True ease is so complete you don't notice it

fix.display_text: To be unconscious of one's feet implies that the shoes are easy. To be unconscious of a waist implies that the girdle is easy. The intelligence being unconscious of positive and negative implies that the heart is at ease. No modifications within, no yielding to influences without,--this is ease under all conditions. And he who beginning with ease, is never not at ease, is unconscious of the ease of ease.

items.plain: Wherever there is union there is separation; completion, destruction; purity, oppression; honour, contempt; doing, undoing; openness, scheming; and wherever there is no pretence there is still deceit. So how can anything be fixed?
items.core_idea: Every condition carries its opposite; nothing is fixed

items.plain: The human part of us is what holds us back, and the human part of others is what causes us sorrow.
items.core_idea: Our humanness hinders us; others' humanness grieves us

items.plain: If an empty boat drifts into yours, even a hot-tempered man won't get angry; if someone is in it, he'll shout and curse. The difference is only the emptiness. If you drifted through life empty, who could hurt you?
items.core_idea: Be empty of self and no one can harm you

items.plain: Praising yourself proves nothing. Achievement brings decline, and fame brings loss. Who can let go of both achievement and fame and become one with everyone else?
items.core_idea: Let go of merit and fame; be one with all

items.plain: A good person's friendship is plain like water; a petty person's is rich like wine. The good one grows warmer; the petty one fades to nothing. Petty friendship starts for no real reason and ends the same way.
items.core_idea: Plain friendship deepens; showy friendship fades

items.plain: Chuang Tzu said he was poor, not miserable. Someone who has the Tao cannot be miserable; ragged clothes and worn-out boots are poverty, not misery.
items.core_idea: With the Tao, poverty is not misery

fix.display_text: "It is poverty, not misery," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "A man who has TAO cannot be miserable. Ragged clothes and old boots make poverty, not misery."

items.plain: Confucius said that hunger, thirst, cold and heat are only shackles on the road of life. They are part of the natural laws of the universe, and he follows his allotted course in obedience to them.
items.core_idea: Hardships are natural laws; follow your course

fix.display_text: "Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat," replied Confucius, "are but as fetters in the path of life. They belong to the natural laws which govern the universe; and in obedience thereto I pass on my allotted course."

items.plain: Confucius said that the work of the world goes on and no one knows why. So how could anyone know its end or its beginning? All that is left to us is to wait.
items.core_idea: We cannot know the cause; we can only wait

items.plain: Chuang Tzu sighed at how creatures harm one another, and said that chasing gain leads to loss.
items.core_idea: Chasing gain leads to loss

items.plain: Chuang Tzu said that while looking after his body, he lost sight of his real self; staring at muddy water, he lost sight of the clear depths.
items.core_idea: Caring for the body, he lost his true self

fix.display_text: "While keeping my physical frame," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "I lost sight of my real self. Gazing at muddy water, I lost sight of the clear abyss."

items.plain: An innkeeper loved his plain partner over his beautiful one: the beauty was so vain she seemed unattractive, the plain one so aware of it she didn't seem plain. Be good without being self-conscious, and you'll be loved everywhere.
items.core_idea: Be good without being conscious of it

items.plain: No sorrow compares with the death of the mind. The death of the body matters less.
items.core_idea: The mind's death is worse than the body's

items.plain: What you admire in me doesn't last. Still, why grieve? Though my old self is always passing away, something remains that does not pass away.
items.core_idea: Beneath the passing self, something endures

items.plain: Lao Tzu said that grazing animals don't mind new pasture and water creatures don't mind a new pond. Small changes are fine as long as the essential thing is left untouched.
items.core_idea: Small changes don't matter if the essence stays

fix.display_text: "Animals," said Lao Tzŭ, "that eat grass do not mind a change of pasture. Creatures that live in water do not mind a change of pond. A slight change may be effected so long as the essential is untouched."

items.plain: Asked how he stayed calm through being appointed and dismissed three times, Sun Shu Ao said office comes and can't be refused, goes and can't be kept. Gaining and losing it lie outside himself, so he feels no disappointment.
items.core_idea: Gain and loss of position lie outside yourself

fix.display_text: Chien Wu said to Sun Shu Ao, "Sir, you have been three times called to office without showing any elation, and you have been three times dismissed without displaying any chagrin. At first, I doubted you; but now I notice that your breathing is perfectly regular. How do you manage thus to control your emotions?" "I am no better than other people," replied Sun Shu Ao. "I regard office when it comes as something which may not be declined; when it goes, as something which cannot be kept. To me both the getting and losing are outside my own self; and therefore I feel no chagrin. How am I better than other people?"

items.plain: Life follows death, and death begins life; who knows where the end is? Life is the gathering of the vital breath and death its scattering. If life and death simply follow each other, why should I complain?
items.core_idea: Life and death follow each other; why complain

items.plain: The universe is deeply beautiful yet says nothing. The seasons follow a fixed law yet make no sound. All creation rests on absolute principles, yet nothing speaks.
items.core_idea: The universe's beauty and order are silent

items.plain: Keep your body disciplined and your gaze fixed on the One, and the peace of God will come down on you. Hold back your knowledge and focus your thoughts on the One, and the holy spirit will live within you.
items.core_idea: Focus on the One and God's peace comes

items.plain: A human life passes like a white horse glimpsed through a crack: here, then gone. One change brings life, another death; creatures cry out and people grieve. Then the soul takes flight and the body follows on the journey home.
items.core_idea: Life flashes past; death is the journey home

items.plain: An eighty-year-old swordsmith never made a mistake. Asked whether it was skill or method, he said concentration: from age twenty he cared about nothing but swords, noticed nothing else, and put all his spare energy into that one craft.
items.core_idea: Mastery comes from total, lifelong concentration

fix.display_text: The man who forged swords for the Minister of War was eighty years of age. Yet he never made the slightest slip in his work. The Minister of War said to him, "Is it your skill, Sir, or have you any method?" "It is concentration," replied the man. "When twenty years old, I took to forging swords. I cared for nothing else. If a thing was not a sword, I did not notice it. I availed myself of whatever energy I did not use in other directions in order to secure greater efficiency in the direction required."

items.plain: Let yourself change only on the outside. On the inside, stay constant and unchanged.
items.core_idea: Adapt outwardly; stay constant within

items.plain: Forests and fields fill me with joy, but sorrow soon returns, and I control neither. Life is a short stop at an inn. There is always more we can't know or do; struggling against that brings grief.
items.core_idea: Fighting life's limits only brings more grief

items.plain: Nan Yung said every choice harms either himself or others, and he sees no way out. Lao Tzu said: you are lost like a child without parents, trying to return to your natural self but unable to find the way.
items.core_idea: Lost in dilemmas, he can't find his natural self

items.plain: If the trouble comes from outside, don't keep fighting it; close the paths into your mind. If it comes from inside, don't struggle against it; shut out everything from outside.
items.core_idea: Don't fight disturbances; close the way in

items.plain: Lao Tzu said that preserving life means keeping all in the One, losing nothing, knowing when to stop and what is enough, minding your own affairs, being free of cares and cleverness: in fact, being like a child.
items.core_idea: To preserve life, be simple like a child

fix.display_text: "The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, to lose nothing, to estimate good and evil without divination, to know when to stop, and how much is enough, to leave others alone and attend to oneself, to be without cares and without knowledge,--to be in fact as a child."

items.plain: People whose hearts are at rest give off a divine light, by which they see themselves as they really are. Only by cultivating that inner rest can anyone reach what is constant.
items.core_idea: A restful heart lets you see yourself truly

items.plain: Those devoted to inner life gain no reputation; those devoted to outward things compete for the top. Quiet practice makes even the humblest shine, while the status-seeker is like a peddler whose tiredness shows through his forced cheer.
items.core_idea: Quiet inner practice shines; chasing status shows strain

items.plain: No weapon is as deadly as human will, and no bandit as powerful as Nature, which nothing in the universe escapes. Yet it is not Nature that does the harm; it is a person's own heart.
items.core_idea: Harm comes from our own heart, not Nature

items.plain: Birth is not a beginning, and death is not an end. There is existence without limit and continuity without a starting point.
items.core_idea: Birth doesn't begin us; death doesn't end us

items.plain: If you want peace, calm your emotions. If you want spirituality, let your mind adapt. If you want to act rightly, go along with what is necessary, because necessity is the sage's Tao.
items.core_idea: Calm emotions, adapt, and accept necessity

items.plain: An exile is glad after days to meet anyone he knew from home, after a month anyone he'd seen there, after a year anyone resembling his countrymen. Being away from your own kind makes you long for them more.
items.core_idea: Absence from your own kind deepens the longing

fix.display_text: "Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. After a month, he was glad to meet any one he had even seen there. And after a year, he was glad to meet any one who was in any way like to his fellow-countrymen. Is not this a case of absence from one's kind increasing the desire to be with them?"

items.plain: Being in a high position doesn't make you a great person, and being in a low one doesn't make you a lesser one.
items.core_idea: Rank does not make anyone high or low

items.plain: Schemers aren't happy without something to worry about, debaters without their arguments, critics without someone to attack. Such people are slaves to things outside themselves.
items.core_idea: Needing outside things to be happy is slavery

items.plain: Farmers, merchants, workers, the greedy, the boastful and the ambitious all depend on their activity; without it they are lost. People can never stop doing, and so they rush to ruin, scattering their life energy for good.
items.core_idea: Endless restless doing drains life away

items.plain: Anyone who wants to find a lost child but won't leave the house is likely to lose the child.
items.core_idea: You can't find what's lost without leaving home

items.plain: At his friend Hui Tzu's grave, Chuang Tzu told of a mason whose feat depended on a partner who never flinched; when the partner died, the feat ended. Since Hui Tzu died, Chuang Tzu has no one to talk with.
items.core_idea: Losing a true friend leaves no one to talk to

items.plain: Sharing your virtue with others is true wisdom; sharing your wealth is counted as merit. Showing off your superiority doesn't win people's hearts; showing yourself as lesser does.
items.core_idea: Humility, not displayed superiority, wins hearts

items.plain: On Monkey Mountain, one monkey showed off before a prince, even catching his arrow, and his guards shot it dead. The prince told his friend: it flaunted its skill in my face and died for it. Don't flaunt your superiority.
items.core_idea: Flaunting your superiority invites destruction

items.plain: A dog isn't good just because it barks well, nor a person good just because he talks well. Greatness needs even more than that; and if doing great things doesn't make you great, it certainly doesn't make you virtuous.
items.core_idea: Talking well or doing great things isn't virtue

items.plain: It is said that wind and sun make the river suffer. But though both act on it, the river is not really harmed: fed from its source, it keeps on flowing.
items.core_idea: Fed from its source, the river keeps flowing

items.plain: Your foot touches only a little ground, yet it is the untrodden ground around it that makes walking possible. Human knowledge is limited, but it is on what we don't know that we rely to reach an understanding of God.
items.core_idea: The unknown is what leads us toward God

items.plain: The old country and the old home delight a wanderer's eyes. Even if almost all of it has become a wilderness, his eyes are still glad to see it.
items.core_idea: Home gladdens the wanderer even in ruins

items.plain: The true sage pays no attention to God, to man, to beginnings or to matter. He moves in step with his times without suffering and takes things as they come without being overwhelmed. How can we become like him?
items.core_idea: The sage takes things as they come, untroubled

items.plain: The rulers of old gave their people credit for every success and took the blame for every failure. Whatever went right was the people's; whatever went wrong was theirs. So when anything fell short, they blamed themselves.
items.core_idea: Good leaders credit others and blame themselves

items.plain: At sixty, Chü Poh Yü changed his mind, calling wrong what he had called right. But who can say today's right won't turn out as wrong as the views of his previous fifty-nine years?
items.core_idea: Today's certainty may be tomorrow's mistake

items.plain: Seasons begin and end. Generations keep changing. Good and bad fortune take turns, bringing sorrow in one place and happiness in another.
items.core_idea: Fortune and seasons turn; nothing stays

items.plain: Someone who stubbornly sees things only from his own point of view may be right in one case and wrong in another.
items.core_idea: One fixed viewpoint is sometimes right, sometimes wrong

items.plain: Danger and safety take turns; good and bad fortune give rise to each other; gathering and scattering go together. You can see this happen. Movement runs forward and bends; exhaustion leads to renewal, and every end brings a new beginning.
items.core_idea: Opposites alternate; every end brings a beginning

items.plain: The cock crows and the dog barks; that much we know. But even the wisest person can't say why one crows and the other barks, or why they make any sound at all.
items.core_idea: We know what happens, not why

fix.display_text: "The cock crows," replied T'ai Kung Tiao, "and the dog barks. So much we know. But the wisest of us could not say why one crows and the other barks, nor guess why they crow or bark at all."

items.plain: Every parent wants devoted children, yet devotion to parents does not necessarily win their love.
items.core_idea: Filial devotion doesn't guarantee being loved

items.plain: As rubbed wood makes fire and clashing forces bring storms, the inner struggle between peace and unrest, good and evil, makes a fire that burns up a person's harmony. The mind can't withstand it, and with it the Tao ends.
items.core_idea: Inner conflict burns away harmony and the Tao

items.plain: Chuang Tzu, poor, asked a prince for grain and was promised silver later. He told of a stranded fish that begged for a pint of water, was promised a river later, and said: just put me in a dried-fish shop.
items.core_idea: Help promised later is no help to the desperate

items.plain: Lao Lai Tzu said: one generation's wounds are already too much, yet you would take on the sorrows of all time. Aren't you tired? Do you have the strength for that?
items.core_idea: Don't take on the sorrows of all time

fix.display_text: "The wounds of one generation being too much," answered Lao Lai Tzŭ, "you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Are you not weary? Is your strength equal to the task?"

items.plain: Even great wisdom faces countless traps; a fish safe from nets still has pelicans. Drop small cleverness and great wisdom will shine; put away goodness and you'll be naturally good. Children learn speech by living among speakers.
items.core_idea: Drop cleverness and effortful goodness; be natural

items.plain: Rest heals the sick, rubbing the eyelids smooths old wrinkles, and quiet clears away worry. But these remedies are only for those who need them; people free of these troubles pay them no attention.
items.core_idea: Remedies matter only to those who need them

items.plain: A trap is for the fish and a snare for the rabbit; once caught, the tool can be forgotten. Words are for ideas; once the idea arrives, the words can be forgotten. Where is someone beyond words to talk with?
items.core_idea: Words are tools; forget them once meaning arrives

items.plain: Tsêng Tzu held office twice and felt differently each time. While his parents were alive, he was happy on a small salary; later, with a large salary but his parents gone, he was sad.
items.core_idea: Loved ones matter more than money

items.plain: In life there are differences between people, but death makes us all equal.
items.core_idea: Death makes everyone equal

items.plain: Lao Tzu said: you look arrogant; who would want to live with you? Someone truly pure behaves as if stained, and someone rich in virtue behaves as if he had too little.
items.core_idea: True virtue acts as if it lacks virtue

items.plain: Offered the empire, Shan Chüan said he is a small part of the universe: dressing for the seasons, farming, working dawn to dusk, resting after harvest, content and light-hearted. Why trouble with an empire? You don't know me.
items.core_idea: A contented simple life needs no empire

items.plain: A prince was wearing himself out fighting over land. His adviser showed him that he wouldn't trade a hand for the whole world, so his body matters far more than this land, yet he exhausts body and soul over it.
items.core_idea: Don't wear out your life for lesser things

items.plain: The true sage weighs the reasons for all he does. Shooting at a bird with a priceless pearl makes the world laugh, because it gives up the greater for the lesser. Surely life is worth even more than that pearl.
items.core_idea: Life is worth more than any prize

items.plain: Lieh Tzu, poor and hungry, refused food sent by a minister, despite his wife's protest. The minister acted only on what others said about him, he explained; if others spoke ill of him, the minister would act on that too.
items.core_idea: Don't accept favours based only on others' opinions

items.plain: Yüan Hsien said that having no wealth is called being poor, while learning without being able to practise is called being sick. He is simply poor; there is nothing wrong with him.
items.core_idea: Poverty is not failure; unpractised learning is

items.plain: Poor Yen Hui declined office: his fields fed and clothed him, his lute and study made him happy. Confucius praised him: the contented don't chase gain, and those who cultivate the inner self feel no shame without position.
items.core_idea: Contentment frees you from chasing gain and status

fix.display_text: "Come hither," said Confucius to Yen Hui. "Your family is poor, and your position lowly. Why not go into official life?" "I do not wish to," replied Yen Hui. "I have fifty acres of land beyond the city walls, which are enough to supply me with food. Ten more within the walls provide me with clothes. My lute gives me all the amusement I want; and the study of your doctrines keeps me happy enough. I do not desire to go into official life." "Bravo! well said!" cried Confucius with beaming countenance. "I have heard say that those who are contented do not entangle themselves in the pursuit of gain. That those who have really obtained do not fear the contingency of loss. That those who devote themselves to cultivation of the inner man, though occupying no position, feel no shame."

items.plain: A prince's body was in the country but his heart in the city. Value life above all, he was told, and gain loses its pull. If you can't, follow your nature; forcing yourself beyond your ability doubles the harm.
items.core_idea: Forcing yourself beyond your nature doubles the harm

items.plain: Told they had failed, Confucius said failure means failing in the Tao, and holding to the Tao in a disordered age is no failure. Like pines thriving in frost and snow, he counts his hardship a blessing.
items.core_idea: Hardship, like winter, brings out true strength

items.plain: The ancients who found the Tao were equally happy in success and failure; their happiness didn't depend on either. With the Tao, success and failure became just links in a chain, like cold, heat, wind and rain.
items.core_idea: With the Tao, success and failure don't decide happiness

items.plain: At most a person lives a hundred years. Remove the time lost to sickness, mourning and trouble, and only four or five days a month are left for laughter. Next to everlasting Heaven and Earth, a life is a flash.
items.core_idea: Life is brief, with few days for laughter

items.plain: A ruler's power doesn't make him worthy, and poverty or low rank doesn't make someone unworthy. What separates the worthy from the unworthy is whether their actions are worthy.
items.core_idea: Worth is shown by actions, not rank

items.plain: Don't leave the path of virtue, and don't try to engineer your own good deeds, or your effort will be wasted. Don't chase wealth or aim at success, or you will throw away what connects you to God.
items.core_idea: Chasing wealth and success cuts your link to God

items.plain: The wise man acts for the common good without overstepping proper limits. So when he has enough, he doesn't try for more; he has no use for more, so he doesn't look for it.
items.core_idea: The wise stop seeking once they have enough

fix.display_text: "The wise man," answered Complacency, "acts for the common weal, in pursuit of which he does not overstep due limits. Wherefore, if there is a sufficiency, he does not strive for more. He has no use for more, and accordingly does not seek it."

items.plain: Happiness is found in being content. Too much of anything is always a curse, and above all too much wealth.
items.core_idea: Happiness lies in contentment; excess is a curse

fix.display_text: "Happiness," said Complacency, "is to be found in contentment. Too much is always a curse, most of all in wealth."

items.plain: Knowing your faults but not fixing them, and being warned but only going further wrong: that is stubbornness.
items.core_idea: Ignoring known faults and warnings is obstinacy

items.plain: A man afraid of his shadow and footsteps tried to outrun them, but they kept up. Thinking he was too slow, he ran until he died. He never realised that resting in the shade, keeping still, would have ended both.
items.core_idea: Running from yourself only exhausts you; be still

items.plain: Take careful care of your body, guard your natural purity, and leave outside matters to others; then you won't get entangled. But instead of improving yourself, you are trying to improve other people, and that is dealing with the external.
items.core_idea: Improve yourself instead of trying to fix others

items.plain: True grief mourns in silence. True anger commands respect without words. True friendship is harmony that needs no smiles.
items.core_idea: True feeling needs no outward show

items.plain: The true sage rests in what truly gives rest, not in what doesn't. The world rests in what doesn't give rest, and not in what does.
items.core_idea: Most people seek rest where none is found

items.plain: The sage treats certainties as uncertain, so he never takes up arms; most people treat uncertainties as certain, so they are always ready to fight. Getting used to fighting makes you fight at every provocation; relying on force, you perish.
items.core_idea: Holding certainties loosely keeps you from conflict

items.plain: Alas, human knowledge can split a hair, yet it cannot reach lasting peace.
items.core_idea: Knowledge is precise but cannot bring peace

items.plain: Outward punishments come from metal and wood; inner punishments come from anxiety and remorse. Fools are punished outwardly with chains and blades, while others are eaten up inside by warring emotions. Only the pure and perfect person escapes both.
items.core_idea: Anxiety and remorse are inner punishments

items.plain: Have you seen a sacrificial ox, decked in ribbons and fed richly? When it is led to slaughter at the temple, wouldn't it gladly trade places with some neglected calf?
items.core_idea: Pampered honour can lead to sacrifice

items.plain: As Chuang Tzu was dying, his disciples wanted a grand funeral. He said: with Heaven and Earth as my coffin, the sun, moon and stars as my ornaments, and all creation as my escort, isn't my funeral already prepared?
items.core_idea: All creation is funeral enough

items.plain: Not craving fame after death, not trying to dazzle the world, not posing as humanity's benefactor, but being strict with yourself and forgiving of others' faults: that was the Tao of the ancients.
items.core_idea: Be strict with yourself, lenient with others

items.plain: Serving the public without faction or selfishness, moving freely, taking things as they come, with no regret for the past or worry about the future, favouring no one and friendly with all: that was the Tao of the ancients.
items.core_idea: No regret, no worry, taking things as they come

items.plain: Don't take a fixed position, and let outside things look after themselves. When moving, be like water; when still, like a mirror; when responding, like an echo.
items.core_idea: Move like water, rest like a mirror

items.plain: Being generous in sympathy toward all creation, and not aggressive toward other people, can be called perfection.
items.core_idea: Sympathy for all, aggression toward none, is perfection

items.plain: Silence, formlessness, change and impermanence; now life, now death; heaven and earth merged; the soul leaving for who knows where, as all things go in turn, never to return: this was the Tao of the ancients.
items.core_idea: All things change and pass, never returning

items.plain: My soul has room to take in God completely. I am certain that nothing is as near to me as God. God is nearer to me than I am to myself, and my existence depends on his presence.
items.core_idea: God is nearer to me than I am to myself

items.plain: Serving God from fear is good, from love better, from fear and love together best. A peaceful life in God is good, bearing pain patiently better, but peace in the middle of pain is best of all.
items.core_idea: Best of all is peace in the midst of pain

items.plain: You can be aware of God praying in a field or in church. If you feel him more in a quiet place, that is your shortcoming, not God's, for he is present everywhere. Whoever knows God everywhere knows him rightly.
items.core_idea: Knowing God rightly means finding him everywhere

items.plain: No one wants anything as eagerly as God wants people to know him. God is always ready; we are not. God is near, we are far; God is within, we are without; God is friendly, we are estranged.
items.core_idea: God is always near; we are the ones far away

items.plain: A wife who lost an eye feared her husband would love her less, so he put out one of his own to show his love. Likewise, people could hardly believe God loved them until God took on human nature.
items.core_idea: God became human to show his love

fix.display_text: There were a certain man and wife; the woman by accident lost an eye, and was sorely troubled thereat. Her husband then said to her, "Wife, why are you troubled?" She answered, "It is not the loss of my eye that troubles me, but the thought that you may love me less on account of that loss." He said, "I love you all the same." Not long after he put one of his own eyes out, and came to his wife and said, "Wife, that you may believe I love you, I have made myself like you: I, too, now, have only one eye." So men could hardly believe that God loved them till God put one of His eyes out, that is took upon Himself human nature, and was made man.
fix.reason: Misplaced space around closing quotation mark

items.plain: Whichever way the earth flees from heaven, it meets heaven, which makes it fruitful whether it wants this or not. So God does with people: whoever tries to escape him flies into his arms; every corner is open to him.
items.core_idea: No one can escape God; fleeing leads to him
